title: The lab, the factory and the dentist
content:
At the lab, they don’t know the right answer. They are explorers and scientists. If you’re not failing, you’re not trying hard enough. The work at the lab requires mutual support, shared information and a commitment to the process of discovery.

At the factory, the answer is known. It’s productivity that’s being pursued. Do it a little faster, a little better and a little more reliably than yesterday. Cut costs. Repeat.

And the dentist? It’s not rote work, but it’s not a dance with the unknown. Meet a client, diagnosis the problem and do the work efficiently as well. Different than yesterday, but it certainly rhymes.

Where do you work?

It could be that you’re getting exactly what you signed up for.

title: Many Space Missions Are Searching for Life Beyond Earth—But Are We Prepared for the Fallout If They Succeed?
content:
Microbes from space have fueled the plots of science fiction mainstays like “[Project Hail Mary](https://theconversation.com/project-hail-mary-explores-unique-forms-of-life-in-space-5-essential-reads-on-searching-for-aliens-that-look-nothing-like-life-on-earth-278757)” and “[The Andromeda Strain](https://michaelcrichton.com/works/the-andromeda-strain/).” But with more space missions launching each year, finding[extraterrestrial life in a microbial form](https://doi.org/10.17226/25252)is becoming more plausible. What will the response be back here on Earth if—or when—scientists discover extraterrestrial microbes? Will the international policy and security communities be prepared for the fallout?

Featured Video

When you hear about extraterrestrial life, your mind may go to intelligent life, like the kind present in a lot of Hollywood science fiction. But even the confirmation of microbial life that originated somewhere other than on Earth—which is much more likely—would be a paradigm-shifting event. Thinking about what these consequences might look like early on can help nations and the international community prepare.

Our team is interested in this question. We’re made up of a full professor of international affairs, who earned a Ph.D. in chemistry, and whose expertise is on[how emerging science and technologies](https://inta.gatech.edu/people/person/margaret-e-kosal)could affect global conflict and cooperation, as well as an emerging scholar in[space policy and security](https://www.linkedin.com/in/dayana-alagirova/)and an expert on[social and political implications](https://rsis.edu.sg/profile/karryl-kim-sagun-trajano/)of frontier technologies, such as AI, space, quantum and energy sources.

Multiple Mars landers have identified[large amounts of frozen and liquid water](https://doi.org/10.1089/ast.2021.0104), essential for life, on the red planet. Samples retrieved by[Japan’s Hayabusa2 spacecraft](https://www.isas.jaxa.jp/en/missions/spacecraft/current/hayabusa2.html)from a near-Earth asteroid[revealed the presence of uracil](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-36904-3), part of RNA, which is a building block of life. Uncrewed space probes like NASA’s[Europa Clipper](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/europa-clipper/)and the European Space Agency’s[Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer](https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Juice)are on their way to conduct detailed reconnaissance of the planet’s moons and to investigate whether they have conditions suitable for life.

[Video 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3HN_zx4JJfM)

Along with[data from the James Webb Space Telescope](https://theconversation.com/to-search-for-alien-life-astronomers-will-look-for-clues-in-the-atmospheres-of-distant-planets-and-the-james-webb-space-telescope-just-proved-its-possible-to-do-so-184828)and future missions targeting[Saturn’s icy moon Enceladus](https://www.esa.int/About_Us/ESAC/Saturn_s_moon_Enceladus_top_target_for_ESA), the likelihood of discovering extraterrestrial microbial life has increased substantially.

**A Governance Challenge**

The discovery of microbial life would expose significant gaps in international governance related to space.

While there are some existing international agreements, including the[Outer Space Treaty](https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introouterspacetreaty.html), that provide space law guidelines, these are ill-equipped to address the complexities posed by extraterrestrial biology.

The[Outer Space Treaty](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315610139), established in 1967,[dictates that](https://theconversation.com/space-law-hasnt-been-changed-since-1967-but-the-un-aims-to-update-laws-and-keep-space-peaceful-171351)countries should use outer space peacefully. It also states that[no single nation may claim ownership](https://theconversation.com/property-and-sovereignty-in-space-as-countries-and-companies-take-to-the-stars-they-could-run-into-disputes-245334)or exert sovereignty over parts of outer space or celestial bodies such as the Moon.

However, it doesn’t have much to say about who can own extraterrestrial organisms or what to do about biosecurity risks. It doesn’t have direction for who can use, preserve or destroy living things, such as bacteria or fungi, that may be discovered in space.

**Historical Analogies and Future Pathways**

While people have yet to discover extraterrestrial life of any kind, there are some major geopolitical events that can help researchers understand what the consequences might look like.

While the[space race of the 1950s and ’60s](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actaastro.2018.04.053)led to exploration of the Moon, it was driven by a Cold War power struggle between two nations back on Earth. Instead of coming together to explore space, both countries experienced a[renewed sense of nationalism](https://doi.org/10.29173/cons29377). They used the new discoveries that came from the space race to invest in their military capabilities.

On the other hand, researchers can look at how states respond to[asteroid threats](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.spacepol.2025.101726). Since an asteroid could pose a[truly existential threat](https://doi.org/10.1080/00396330802456502)from space, preventing the worst-case scenario requires cooperation and thinking ahead.

Astronomers have built a[global, collaborative network](https://iawn.net/)to monitor for and sound the alarm about any potential threats. This network has shown that nations can put aside terrestrial rivalries to work together if they perceive something from space as a truly existential threat.

The[International Space Station](https://www.nasa.gov/international-space-station/)is another example showing how nations that are[competing great powers on Earth](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.spacepol.2018.07.003)work together to cooperate in space. Countries have collaborated to solve issues on the International Space Station that have specific, short-term and clearly identified goals.

These examples show a range of possible reactions to the discovery of space microbes. The situation could renew space races between competing countries and lead to militarization, or it could create unprecedented cooperation.

**Potential Outcomes**

We’ve identified three main possible outcomes to the discovery of microbial extraterrestrial life.

First, there’s a cooperative outcome, reminiscent of the[asteroid threat network](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actaastro.2018.07.023)or the[International Space Station](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.spacepol.2004.06.007). Here, nations collaborate to regulate research, share data, protect the planet or advance specific interests they share.

This pathway isn’t inherently benign or malignant. It could entail expanding the roles of international organizations or[creating new legal instruments](https://cba.org/sections/air-and-space-law/resources/from-sea-to-sky-can-the-law-of-the-sea-act-as-a-successful-model-for-a-future-asteroid-mining-legal/).

Second there’s a competitive outcome, characterized by strategic rivalry between countries. Like in the space race, nations could[fight to be technologically superior](https://www.newamerica.org/insights/the-rise-of-techno-nationalism/).[They might try to monopolize access](https://doi.org/10.1016/0959-3780(93)90006-7)to the extraterrestrial microbes or to leverage biological discoveries from the microbes for their own economic or military advantage.

Scientific breakthroughs derived from extraterrestrial organisms could lead to innovations in medicine, agriculture, energy and beyond. However, the organisms could also be weaponized, intentionally or otherwise, which would amplify[biosecurity risks](https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biab115). In this sense, the discovery of microbial life could create a new form of technological competition, one that merges space exploration with biological research and development.

The[increasing role of private companies](https://doi.org/10.1080/00963402.2021.2014229), such as SpaceX, complicates this dynamic. These companies receive contracts from the government,[blurring the lines](https://theconversation.com/a-plan-b-for-space-on-the-risks-of-concentrating-national-space-power-in-private-hands-275618)between commercial civilian and strategic activities.

For example, around[60% of all satellites](https://www.space.com/spacex-starlink-satellites.html)currently orbiting the Earth belong to SpaceX’s Starlink subsidiary. The company can—and has—chosen to[block access](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/02/25/elon-musk-russian-army-starlink-00793742)selectively, in alignment with its political priorities. When commercial interests and national priorities diverge, who has access versus who is denied access can be uncertain.

[Research around biopiracy](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/539065/biopiracy-by-vandana-shiva/)may come into play. Biopiracy is a term that applies to two primary issues: the[patenting of indigenous knowledge](https://theconversation.com/patents-based-on-traditional-knowledge-are-often-biopiracy-a-new-international-treaty-will-finally-combat-this-231272)or the patenting of natural resources, such as microbes, for profit.[The Budapest Treaty](https://www.wipo.int/en/web/treaties/registration/budapest/index)prohibits claiming ownership of a naturally occurring microbe on Earth, but there’s no equivalent for microbes in space.

Third is an isolationist outcome, in which states could sever their involvement in international cooperation due to[biosecurity concerns](https://biodefensecommission.org/is-the-u-s-ready-for-extraterrestrials-not-if-theyre-microbes-opinion-2/)or political distrust. The potential for unknown biological risks, however minimal, could trigger[precautionary restrictions on data sharing](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12879-024-09054-0), which limits international collaboration.

Countries may lose or gain allies as they grapple with whether the microbe could cause harm to humans or the environment, or be developed into a biological weapon.

Emerging technologies will also shape these outcomes.[Artificial intelligence and machine learning](https://doi.org/10.1177/15311074261463025)are already integral to scientific research. Scientists use them to[process astronomical data](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10686-021-09827-4)and[identify potential biosignatures](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2307149120).[Nanotechnology](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-97-6184-5_12)and[advances in the life sciences and engineering](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.orbis.2020.08.008)could allow researchers to study, modify or exploit extraterrestrial microbes, if they’re given access to them.

Countries will have to prepare not only for the scientific implications of discovery but also for its societal and political reverberations. The politicization of scientific discoveries from the microbes could complicate or change how countries respond domestically and at the international scale. Misinformation about the microbes[could shape policy and public response](https://doi.org/10.1080/1369118X.2022.2085615).

**Preparing for the Unprecedented**

The discovery of extraterrestrial microbial life would not merely mark a scientific milestone. It would be a geopolitical event.

Rather than attempting to predict a singular outcome, policymakers could adopt[scenario-based planning](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/162919/the-art-of-the-long-view-by-peter-schwartz/)approaches in the meantime to anticipate and prepare for a range of possibilities. In these approaches, participants explore multiple futures through structured activities similar to professional or military wargaming or[path games](https://inta.gatech.edu/courses/syllabus/202102/34850), in which they explore multiple outcomes systematically to test strategies, to plan and to analyze potential outcomes under realistic uncertainty.

In our view, the question is not whether humanity will discover life beyond Earth, but whether it is prepared for the consequences when it does. ![Image 1](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# How to Reconcile Your Most Painful Mistakes: The Life-Shaping Difference Between Regret and Remorse

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 36: How to Reconcile Your Most Painful Mistakes: The Life-Shaping Difference Between Regret and Remorse](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/bookofhumanemotions_smith.jpg?fit=320%2C488&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/dp/1781251290/?tag=braipick-20)

You know it, that awful moment your coherent self-image shatters and a part of you, shadowy and untended, splits off to cause harm and havoc as the rest of you watches helplessly, wincing. You know the next moment, too — the desperate wish for an undo button you know cannot be had, no matter your protestations and prostrations.

It is a seductive dream, to have [an unregetting life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/03/11/regret/), but it is also a dangerous dream, for it dooms us to the living nightmare of perfection, that punitive negation of our humanity. If we didn’t shudder at our own missteps, we could never wish to leap higher. How achingly beautiful to be reminded that we are not cold algorithms whose very reason for being is to execute commands perfectly; that we are creatures whose imperfection is precisely what makes them perfect miracles of flesh and feeling. Our errors are the source-code of our self-transcendence.

Barring denial and dissociation, there are two ways to relate to our mistakes. Regret, rooted in rumination, is the desperate wish for an undo button — a wish that, however ardent, is hollow of consequence. Remorse, rooted in reflection, is the actionable desire for a redo — the drive, intentional and directional, to transform the revelations of reflection into a new working theory of doing better. Regret is a turbine of self-destruction, remorse an engine of renewal.

[![Image 37](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/whale_maria.jpg?resize=680%2C850&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/03/19/reweaving-the-rainbow/)

Art from [_Reweaving the Rainbow_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/03/19/reweaving-the-rainbow/)

Drawing on the etymological and cultural heritage of both words, historian Tiffany Watt Smith offers a revelatory distinction between the two, both subtle and profound, in [**_The Book of Human Emotions: An Encyclopedia of Feeling from Anger to Wanderlust_**](https://www.amazon.com/dp/1781251290/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://search.worldcat.org/title/960301575)), which also gave us that wonderful [lexicon of difficult emotions from around the world](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/08/24/book-of-human-emotions/). She writes:

> The regret of the past was not the same as our won. From the Old French _regrés_ (sorrows or disappointments), when the word seems to have first entered the English language in the 1400s it described grief felt at the loss of a person, or one’s place in the world. One distinctive difference was that regret was also a kind of performance, an often-heightened expression of sorrow. The “making of regrets,” or _regrettes_, was a pious yet clamouring affair: the lamentations at a wake, the weeping at funerals. In the sixteenth century — the moment historians associate with the birth of the modern concept of an interiorised self — regret began to harden into its contemporary meaning as a self-reproach, a private anguish felt looking back at some action you wish you’d not committed — or that you wish you had. It was at this time that the threat of this hidden torture, rather than punishment in the hereafter, became a deterrent favoured by parents and preachers alike. “For this deed thou shalt for anguish fret,” warned the Calvinist parliamentarian Francis Rous in 1598 and “feed thy wombe with woe and deepe regret.”
> 
> 
> Today, regret remains firmly entrenched as a private emotional experience… The regrets we feel most sorely are often the ones that jar hardest with our sense of self.

The real value of regret, Watt Smith observes, is to remind us of “the ambivalence which haunts all of our lives” — that disquieting evidence of [the parts we live with](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/04/10/parts/).

But because regret is at bottom “a kind of desire for something different to have happened,” it is an emotion shot dead by time’s arrow. Hannah Arendt knew this when she considered [the only antidote to the irreversibility of life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/07/14/hannah-arendt-forgiveness/) — not regret but redemptive action.

[![Image 38](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/jacquelineayer_paperflowertree5.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/08/30/the-paper-flower-tree-jacqueline-ayer/)

Art by Jacqueline Ayer from [_The Paper-Flower Tree_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/08/30/the-paper-flower-tree-jacqueline-ayer/)

The fulcrum of such action, Watt Smith argues, is remorse. With an eye to the scorching self-blame we feel when we first recognize our harmful missteps, she writes:

> Remorse arrives when the initial flare of anger calms, when the reality of what we’ve said or done clumps in the throat. Unlike the whirring and suffocation of regret, remorse is urgent and wild. Full of terror, flecked with love, it’s a desire to preserve our bond with the person we’ve hurt… Remorse, then, is most clearly defined as an urgent desire to _do_ something. To make amends, to attempt to heal the one we’ve harmed. Because, unlike shame, which is a horror of something we _are_, remorse involves something _done_, and urges us to correct it. In this sense, remorse is both extremely painful and full of striving and hopefulness too.

Remorse, however, is haunted by the specter of regret, which is inherently an act of selfing — a spiral of rumination borrowing into the substrate of our deepest self-doubt. “Excessive remorse,” Watt Smith cautions, may “lead to disproportionate acts, causing more grief, rather than less” — a haunting reminder that [our morality hinges on unselfing](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/10/21/iris-murdoch-unselfing/), and the purpose of reflecting on our errors is not to allay our self-blame but to effect repair and healing for those we have harmed, the catalyst for which is correctly calibrated remorse.

Couple with dissident poet turned president Václav Havel, writing from prison, on [how to hold your greatest failure](https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/05/11/havel-failure/), then revisit Ellen Bass’s benediction of a poem [“How to Apologize.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/11/28/how-to-apologize-ellen-bass/)

# The Most Important Thing to Remember About Your Mother

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 36: The Most Important Thing to Remember About Your Mother](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/floridascottmaxwell_themeasureofmydays.jpg?fit=320%2C492&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Measure-My-Days-Enduring-Celebration/dp/0140051643/?tag=braipick-20)

One of the hardest realizations in life, and one of the most liberating, is that our mothers are neither saints nor saviors — they are just people who, however messy or painful our childhood may have been, and however complicated the adult relationship, have loved us the best way they knew how, with the cards they were dealt and the tools they had.

It is a whole life’s work to accept this elemental fact, and a life’s triumph to accept it not with bitterness but with love.

How to make that liberating shift of perspective is what the playwright, suffragist, and psychologist **Florida Scott-Maxwell** (September 14, 1883–March 6, 1979) considers in a passage from her 1968 autobiography [**_The Measure of My Days_**](https://www.amazon.com/Measure-My-Days-Enduring-Celebration/dp/0140051643/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://www.worldcat.org/title/4514970)).

[![Image 37](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/Lily_by_MariaPopova.jpg?resize=680%2C850&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/kinship6212122_print?curator=brainpicker)

_Kinship_ by Maria Popova. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/kinship6212122_print?curator=brainpicker).)

She writes:

> A mother’s love for her children, even her inability to let them be, is because she is under a painful law that the life that passed through her must be brought to fruition. Even when she swallows it whole she is only acting like any frightened mother cat eating its young to keep it safe.

In a sentiment that calls to mind Kahlil Gibran’s insight into [the delicate balance of intimacy and independence](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/09/27/kahlil-gibran-the-prophet-love-marriage/) essential for romantic love — which is [always an echo of our formative attachments](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/12/04/general-theory-of-love-music-emotion/) — she adds:

> It is not easy to give closeness and freedom, safety plus danger.

[![Image 38](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/crescendo-int-MP89.jpg?w=1200&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/03/20/crescendo-quintavalle-sanna/)

Art by Alessandro Sanna from [_Crescendo_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/03/20/crescendo-quintavalle-sanna/)

With a wary eye to the brunt of parental expectation under which all children live, well into adulthood, she writes:

> No matter how old a mother is she watches her middle-aged children for signs of improvement. It could not be otherwise for she is impelled to know that the seeds of value sown in her have been winnowed. She never outgrows the burden of love, and to the end she carries the weight of hope for those she bore. Oddly, very oddly, she is forever surprised and even faintly wronged that her sons and daughters are just people, for many mothers hope and half expect that their newborn child will make the world better, will somehow be a redeemer. Perhaps they are right, and they can believe that the rare quality they glimpsed in the child is active in the burdened adult.

Perhaps that glimpse is what Maurice Sendak meant when he observed that life is largely a matter of [“having your child self intact and alive and something to be proud of.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/01/21/maurice-sendak-studs-terkel/)

Complement with Kahlil Gibran’s [advice on children](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/09/09/on-children-kahlil-gibran/), the pioneering psychologist Donald Winnicott on [the mother’s contribution to society](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/08/winnicott-mothers-contribution-to-society/), and Alison Bechdel’s superb Winnicott-inspired [_Are You My Mother?_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/09/alison-bechdel-are-you-my-mother-design-matters-interview/), then savor [_My Mother’s Eyes_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/01/22/my-mothers-eyes-jenny-wright/) — a soulful animated short film about loss and the unbreakable bonds of love — and Mary Gaitskill’s poignant advice on [how to move through life when your parents are dying](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/11/11/when-your-parents-are-dying-mary-gaitskill/).

# How to Handle Provocation: Bertrand Russell’s Remarkable Response to a Fascist

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 35: How to Handle Provocation: Bertrand Russell’s Remarkable Response to a Fascist](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/lifeofbertrandrussell.jpg?fit=320%2C480&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Life-Bertrand-Russell-Ronald-Clark/dp/1448200830/?tag=braipick-20)

“To approach someone else convincingly you must do so with open arms and head held high, and your arms can’t be open unless your head _is_ high,” the Lebanese-born French writer Amin Maalouf wrote in his timeless, increasingly timely [reflection on how to disagree](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/10/09/amin-maalouf-identity-criticism/). It is in times as divisive as ours and as sundered by conflicting perspectives that the mastery of such intelligent, kind-hearted, and considered disagreement emerges as a supreme art of living. To respond in a reactive culture, to marry firm moral conviction with a spirit of goodwill and the porousness necessary for appraising other perspectives in order to evolve one’s own, is a Herculean feat of character.

And yet there are instances in which it is unsound to engage with another whose values are so antithetical to one’s own that the collision is bound to shatter one’s sanity rather than build common ground. To recognize those rare instances and choose to stand down is an act of moral courage rather than moral weakness, and no one has articulated that difficult courage with more intellectual elegance and moral grace than the great English philosopher [Bertrand Russell](https://themarginalian.org/tag/bertrand-russell/) (May 18, 1872–February 2, 1970) — a formidable intellect animated by an extraordinary generosity of spirit, awarded the Nobel Prize for [“his varied and significant writings in which he champions humanitarian ideals and freedom of thought.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/09/21/bertrand-russell-nobel-prize-acceptance-speech/)

[![Image 36: bertrandrussell3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/bertrandrussell3.jpg?resize=680%2C357&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Life-Bertrand-Russell-Ronald-Clark/dp/1448200830/?tag=braipick-20)

Bertrand Russell

In January of 1962, Russell received a series of letters from an unlikely correspondent — Sir Oswald Mosley, who had founded the British Union of Fascists thirty years earlier. Mosley was inviting — or, rather, provoking — Russell to engage in a debate, in which he could persuade the moral philosopher of the merits of fascism. Russell’s considered and morally unflinching response, included in Ronald Clark’s excellent biography [**_The Life of Bertrand Russell_**](https://www.amazon.com/Life-Bertrand-Russell-Ronald-Clark/dp/1448200830/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](http://www.worldcat.org/title/life-of-bertrand-russell/oclc/1916184&referer=brief_results)), stands as a manifesto for the right not to engage in a debate with a counterpart so morally misaligned with oneself as to guarantee not only the self-defeating futility of such engagement but its detrimental cost to one’s own sanity.

Shortly before his 90th birthday, Russell writes:

> Dear Sir Oswald,
> 
> 
> Thank you for your letter and for your enclosures. I have given some thought to our recent correspondence. It is always difficult to decide on how to respond to people whose ethos is so alien and, in fact, repellent to one’s own. It is not that I take exception to the general points made by you but that every ounce of my energy has been devoted to an active opposition to cruel bigotry, compulsive violence, and the sadistic persecution which has characterised the philosophy and practice of fascism.
> 
> 
> I feel obliged to say that the emotional universes we inhabit are so distinct, and in deepest ways opposed, that nothing fruitful or sincere could ever emerge from association between us.
> 
> 
> I should like you to understand the intensity of this conviction on my part. It is not out of any attempt to be rude that I say this but because of all that I value in human experience and human achievement.
> 
> 
> Yours sincerely,
> 
> 
> Bertrand Russell

[**_The Life of Bertrand Russell_**](https://www.amazon.com/Life-Bertrand-Russell-Ronald-Clark/dp/1448200830/?tag=braipick-20) remains an invaluable portrait of one of the greatest intellects and largest spirits our civilization has produced. Complement this particular fragment with Blaise Pascal on [how to change minds](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/05/20/blaise-pascal-pensees-persuasion/), Daniel Dennett on [how to criticize with kindness](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/03/28/daniel-dennett-rapoport-rules-criticism/), and Susan Sontag on [the three steps to refuting any argument](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/06/26/susan-sontag-on-censorship/), then revisit Russell on [freedom of thought](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/18/bertrand-russell-free-thought-propaganda-doubt/), [what “the good life” really means](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/02/03/bertrand-russell-immortality-good-life/), [why “fruitful monotony” is essential for happiness](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/01/21/bertrand-russell-boredom-conquest-of-happiness/), [the nature of time](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/13/bertrand-russell-mysticism-logic-time/), and [the four motives driving all human behavior](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/09/21/bertrand-russell-nobel-prize-acceptance-speech/).

# The Power of Being a Threshold Person: Liminality, Communitas, and the Anti-structures of Possibility

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 36: The Power of Being a Threshold Person: Liminality, Communitas, and the Anti-structures of Possibility](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/ritualprocess_turner.jpg?fit=320%2C483&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/What-Are-People-Wendell-Berry/dp/1582434875/?tag=braipick-20)

“All things are so very uncertain, and that’s exactly what makes me feel reassured,” one of the Moomins observes in Tove Jansson’s [masterwork of philosophy disguised as a children’s book](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/09/29/too-ticky-quotes-tove-jansson/). It takes a great spaciousness and sobriety of spirit to be vitalized rather than paralyzed by uncertainty. Most of the time, we brace behind structures of certainty to keep the native chaos of the universe, the fundamental indeterminacy and unpredictability of life, from drowning us in helplessness. But each time we part the bars of conviction and opinion to step out from this cell of certitude, or are evicted from it by some existential cataclysm, we discover that the most interesting parts of life, the most fulfilling experiences, the richest relationships, are found in the spaces between categories, in the unclassifiable, the unnameable, the deliriously disorienting.

[![Image 37](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Woodpecker1.jpg?resize=680%2C1052&ssl=1)](https://www.almanacofbirds.org/)

Art from [_An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days_](https://www.almanacofbirds.org/). (Available as [a print](https://society6.com/product/bird-divinations-ivory-billed-woodpecker-about-almanacofbirdsorg_print?curator=brainpicker) and as [stationery cards](https://society6.com/product/bird-divinations-ivory-billed-woodpecker-about-almanacofbirdsorg_cards?curator=brainpicker).)

In 1969, after nearly two decades of living among the Ndembu people of Zambia, the Scottish cultural anthropologist **Victor Turner** (May 28, 1920–December 18, 1983) took up the question of how we classify and declassify life in his classic [**_The Ritual Process: Structure and Anti-Structure_**](https://www.amazon.com/What-Are-People-Wendell-Berry/dp/1582434875/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://search.worldcat.org/title/641307467)).

Terming these fertile in-between spaces _liminality_ — a word coined a generation earlier by the French ethnographer and folklorist Arnold van Gennep from _limen_, Latin for “threshold” — Turner observes that all rites of passage have liminality at their center: the moment between renouncing the familiar fixed point and reincorporating into the transformed state. This is why in every society those who live in liminality — those who either choose to or are forced to exist [in the margins](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/05/18/bell-hooks-margins/) — are those most likely to be catalysts for transformation.

Half a century before Rebecca Solnit insisted in [her epochal manifesto for active hope](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/03/16/rebecca-solnit-hope-in-the-dark-2/) that “power comes from the shadows and the margins,” Turner writes:

> The attributes of liminality or of liminal personae (“threshold people”) are necessarily ambiguous, since this condition and these persons elude or slip through the network of classifications that normally locate states and positions in cultural space. Liminal entities are neither here nor there; they are betwixt and between the positions assigned and arrayed by law, custom, convention… Liminality is frequently likened to death, to being in the womb, to invisibility, to darkness, to bisexuality, to the wilderness, and to an eclipse of the sun or moon.

Liminality is a function of, and made possible by, what Turner terms _communitas_ — the recognition of “an essential and generic human bond, without which there could be no society.” Different from community in that it doesn’t necessarily involve “an area of common living,” communitas is a kind of social anti-structure — an alternative organizing principle to the standard model of society as “a structured, differentiated, and often hierarchical system of politico-legal-economic positions with many types of evaluation, separating [people] in terms of ‘more’ or ‘less.'”

![Image 38](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/CirrocumulusSea_MariaPopova.jpg?resize=680%2C667&ssl=1)

Ursula K. Le Guin, whose daring defiance of gender, race, and class structures was greatly influenced by Turner’s work, captures the contrast perfectly:

> Structure in society… is cognitive, communitas existential; structure provides a model, communitas a potential; structure classifies, communitas reclassifies; structure is expressed in legal and political institutions, communitas in art and religion.

Turner writes:

> Communitas breaks in through the interstices of structure, in liminality; at the edges of structure, in marginality; and from beneath structure, in inferiority. It is almost everywhere held to be sacred or “holy,” possibly because it transgresses or dissolves the norms that govern structured and institutionalized relationships and is accompanied by experiences of unprecedented potency… Instinctual energies are surely liberated by these processes.

Intuition — what we call these “instinctual energies” — may indeed be nothing more than those rare moments when we break the rim of our structured reality and glimpse, however briefly, a truth larger and more fluid than any container can hold, touching within it the sacred liminality of life itself.
